title: SAMSON’S MOTHER WAS TOLD NOT TO DRINK WINE WHILE CARRYING THE CHILD GOD HAD CHOSEN
paragraphs: SAMSON’S MOTHER WAS TOLD NOT TO DRINK WINE WHILE CARRYING THE CHILD GOD HAD CHOSEN

Before Samson ever tore apart a lion, carried the gates of Gaza, loved Delilah, lost his hair, lost his eyes, or brought a Philistine temple crashing down… God was already speaking about his life while he was still in his mother’s womb.
There is something haunting about the beginning of Samson’s story.
Most people remember the muscles.
The lion.
The jawbone.
The gates ripped from the ground.
Delilah.
The haircut.
The betrayal.
The blindness.
The final prayer.
The collapsing temple.
But Scripture begins Samson’s story somewhere far quieter.
Before Samson became strong enough to terrify armies, there was a woman carrying the weight of years of disappointment.
She was barren.
Scripture does not even give us her name.
It introduces her simply as Manoah’s wife.
No child.
No pregnancy.
No little feet running through the house.
No son to carry the family forward.
Then God interrupted the silence.
An angel of the LORD appeared to her and announced that the woman who had been unable to conceive was going to bear a son.
And then came an instruction that is easy to rush past:
“Now therefore beware, I pray thee, and drink not wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing.” — Judges 13:4, KJV
The Hebrew is even more striking:
וְעַתָּה֙ הִשָּׁ֣מְרִי נָ֔א וְאַל־תִּשְׁתִּ֖י יַ֣יִן וְשֵׁכָ֑ר וְאַל־תֹּאכְלִ֖י כָּל־טָמֵֽא
Ve'attah hishameri na, ve'al-tishti yayin vesheikhar, ve'al-tokhli kol-tame.
“Now therefore, please be careful: do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.”
The word יַיִן — yayin means wine.
שֵׁכָר — shekhar refers to strong or intoxicating drink.
But perhaps the word that deserves our attention first is הִשָּׁמְרִי — hishameri.
Be careful.
Guard yourself.
Watch yourself.
Why?
Because something had changed.
She was about to carry something consecrated to God.
The angel continued:

“For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” — Judges 13:5, KJV
Read that again slowly.
From the womb.
Before Samson could understand his calling, God had already spoken over it.
Before he could make a decision, before he could fight a battle, before anyone could applaud his strength or condemn his failures, his life had been touched by divine purpose.
The Hebrew says:
כִּֽי־נְזִ֧יר אֱלֹהִ֛ים יִֽהְיֶ֥ה הַנַּ֖עַר מִן־הַבָּ֑טֶן
Ki-nezir Elohim yihyeh hana'ar min-habaten.
“For the boy shall be a Nazirite of God from the womb.”
נְזִיר — nazir.
One separated.
Consecrated.
Set apart.

This connects Samson’s story with the Nazirite idea described in Numbers 6, although Samson’s unusual lifelong calling in Judges 13 has its own particular features. We should therefore be careful not to force every detail of Numbers 6 onto Samson’s story.
And notice something especially important.
Judges 13 specifically records the command concerning wine and strong drink being given to Samson’s mother while she was carrying him.
That detail matters.
God was not merely announcing what Samson would someday do.
God was preparing the environment into which Samson would be born.
And suddenly this ancient story begins to feel uncomfortable.
Because we love talking about destiny.
We love promises.
We love hearing that God has a purpose.
We love Jeremiah 29:11 printed on coffee mugs.
We love declarations about calling.
But Judges 13 whispers something our generation does not always want to hear:
Sometimes purpose comes with boundaries.
Sometimes calling requires surrender.
Sometimes God says, “I am going to do something through this life,” and then immediately begins rearranging what surrounds that life.
Not because every restriction found in Samson’s story is a universal command for every Christian.
It is not.
Judges 13 is describing a specific divine calling in a specific redemptive-historical situation.
But the principle underneath it should still make us examine ourselves.
What are we unwilling to surrender even when God is calling us closer?
That question goes much deeper than alcohol.
This passage should not be twisted into saying that every Christian must follow Samson’s mother’s dietary instructions.
That would go beyond Scripture.
The deeper confrontation is this:
What happens when the God we call “Lord” touches something we wanted to keep under our own control?
Our habits.
Our relationships.
Our entertainment.
Our secret conversations.
Our appetites.
Our bitterness.
Our pride.
Our money.
Our sexuality.
Our screens.
Our ambitions.
Our hidden compromises.
We sometimes want God’s purpose without God’s authority.
We want anointing without surrender.
Calling without consecration.
Deliverance without discipline.
Resurrection without a cross.
But Jesus never invited people merely to admire Him.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24, KJV
And here is where Samson’s story becomes painfully human.
Because Samson was chosen…
but Samson was not flawless.
Far from it.
The child announced by an angel eventually became a man repeatedly pulled by appetite.
He possessed astonishing physical strength while displaying devastating moral weakness.
He could tear a lion apart.
But some desires inside himself were harder to conquer.
He could defeat enemies surrounding him.
But he struggled with the enemy within him.
And maybe that is why his story still reaches across thousands of years and grabs us by the chest.
Because some of us know exactly what that feels like.
You love God…
but there is something you keep returning to.
You know Scripture…
but there is a private battle nobody sees.
People think you are strong.
They call you faithful.
They come to you for encouragement.
You smile.
You worship.
You post verses.
You tell everyone else, “God is faithful.”
And somewhere behind the screen there is a part of you whispering:
“If they knew what I was fighting, would they still think I was strong?”
Samson knew what it was to carry calling and contradiction in the same body.
And eventually the contradiction became catastrophe.
Delilah entered the story.
The secret was exposed.
The hair was cut.
The Philistines seized him.
His eyes were gouged out.
The mighty Samson became a prisoner.
The man who had once carried city gates on his shoulders was now being led around by others.
Imagine the darkness.
No applause.
No victories.
No crowds celebrating his strength.
Only chains.
Regret.
Memory.
And blindness.
Perhaps he remembered the things his parents had told him.
The angel.
The promise.
The calling.
The consecration.
Perhaps he remembered what his life was supposed to have been.
And there are people reading this who know that kind of grief.
Not blindness.
Not Philistine chains.
Something quieter.
You remember who you used to be with God.
You remember praying differently.
You remember when worship made you cry.
You remember when sin bothered you faster.
You remember when opening the Bible was not an obligation.
You remember when you could feel conviction and respond immediately.
Then something happened.
Maybe slowly.
Maybe secretly.
Maybe repeatedly.
And now you sometimes look at your spiritual life and wonder:
“How did I get here?”
But there is a sentence buried inside Samson’s darkest chapter that sounds almost like God whispering through the ruins.
“But the hair of his head began to grow again after it was shaven.” — Judges 16:22, KJV
The hair began to grow again.
What a sentence.
The consequences had not disappeared.
His eyes did not suddenly return.
His captivity was real.
His failures were real.
His suffering was real.
Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
But the story was not finished.
And neither is yours simply because you have failed.
Samson eventually prayed:
“O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once…” — Judges 16:28, KJV
Listen to that prayer.
Not the voice of the swaggering warrior.
Not the confident champion.
A broken man calling upon God.
“Remember me.”
And God heard him.
This does not make Samson’s sins insignificant.
Grace never requires us to pretend sin was harmless.
Biblical grace is far more powerful than denial.
Grace looks directly at the wreckage and says that sin does not get the final word when a sinner turns toward God.
And that brings us beyond Samson.
Because Samson can point us toward our need for a greater Deliverer.
Samson began to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins.
Samson’s calling was announced before his birth.
Christ’s coming fulfilled promises God had been unfolding across generations.
Samson stretched out his arms in death and killed his enemies.
Jesus stretched out His arms on a Roman cross and prayed for His enemies.
Samson's death brought destruction upon the Philistines gathered around him.
Christ's death accomplished redemption for sinners, and His resurrection proclaimed that death itself would not have the final word.
Samson was a deeply flawed deliverer.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Savior.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings becoming strong enough to rescue themselves.
It is the story of sinners who could not rescue themselves being pursued by a Savior who could.
Maybe your scandal is not Samson’s scandal.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe it lives in browser history.
Maybe it lives in a bottle.
Maybe in bitterness.
Maybe in an affair nobody discovered.
Maybe in pornography.
Maybe in pride dressed like spirituality.
Maybe in resentment toward somebody you have smiled at every Sunday.
Maybe you have been pretending for so long that you almost forgot you were pretending.
Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel calls you.
Not to hide better.
To come into the light.
Not to excuse sin.
To repent.
Not to punish yourself until you feel worthy again.
To trust the One who bore judgment for sinners at the cross.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will take you back.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Christ and calls sinners to repent and believe.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, failure does not have to become your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to rename you.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not own the final sentence.
Your past cannot overrule the blood of Christ.
Your scandal does not outrank His grace.
This is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Repentance is coming home to truth.
It is finally dropping the mask.
Finally opening the locked room.
Finally saying:
“Jesus, this is what I have become. This is what I did. This is what I keep fighting. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me.”
And there is mercy in Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But do not keep running from Jesus.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person realize there is still hope.
Not for an algorithm.
For the person.
The quiet person.
The ashamed person.
The believer who still attends church but feels spiritually numb.
The father carrying a secret battle.
The mother crying after everyone goes to sleep.
The young person convinced one terrible decision ruined everything.
The Christian who thinks God could never use them again.
Because there may come a night when the person who needs to reread it is you.
There is another way you can stand with this ministry as well.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
Scripture gives us no right to say that.
The New Testament teaches generosity that comes from the heart rather than coercion: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful way to use what God has entrusted to us for ministry.
Whether you support financially or not, please pray.
Share Scripture.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
And never confuse supporting a ministry with belonging to Christ.
Your hope is not Gospel Warrior.
Your hope is Jesus.
Jesus can.
A donation cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus can.
Religious activity cannot resurrect a dead heart.
Jesus can.
And perhaps that is the most important thing Samson’s story leaves echoing inside us.
A person can be called and still stumble.
Gifted and still vulnerable.
Strong in public and bleeding in private.
Consecrated and still desperately dependent upon God.
So do not build your identity around how strong you think you are.
Build your life upon Christ.
If you are standing, depend on Him.
If you are slipping, call upon Him.
If you have fallen, repent and turn toward Him.
If shame has blinded you to hope, remember the cross.
And if the enemy keeps whispering that your story ended at the moment of your greatest failure…
remember Samson sitting in the darkness.
Remember the chains.
Remember the regret.
Then remember one quiet sentence:
The hair began to grow again.
Not because Samson deserved another moment of strength.
Because God was not finished accomplishing His purposes.

And for everyone who belongs to Jesus, your confidence is greater still—not in hair growing back, not in human strength returning, but in a crucified and risen Savior whose grace is greater than your ability to destroy yourself.
So come back.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
There is blood enough at Calvary for sinners.
There is grace enough in Christ for the ashamed.
There is forgiveness for those who repent and believe.
There is a Savior whose scars declare that sin is serious, judgment is real, mercy is costly, and redemption was purchased.
And when Jesus takes hold of a ruined story, the scandal may remain part of the testimony…
but it no longer gets to write the ending.
Your darkest chapter may explain where you have been, but only Jesus has the authority to write what grace makes possible next.
